Floods in 2021 Disrupted Dutch Oil & Gas Producers’ Operations, Industry Recalls

AMSTERDAM, June 12 — Severe flooding in the south of the Netherlands in July 2021 caused significant disruptions to the country’s oil and gas producers, leading to weeks-long interruptions at key storage and transport sites, industry officials said in a retrospective assessment.

The floods, triggered by record rainfall along the Maas and its tributaries, inundated large areas of Limburg province and forced the temporary closure of multiple terminals and pipeline routes. Vitol Holding BV and other operators reported impacts to their facilities and supply lines, as floodwaters breached protective barriers and damaged infrastructure.

“Water levels rose rapidly, exceeding all forecasts,” said Jan de Vries, spokesperson for the Dutch Association of Oil & Gas Producers. “Operators had to halt activities to ensure safety, and in some cases, it took more than ten days for water to fully recede so assessments and repairs could begin.”

At the height of the crisis, major terminals in the Venlo and Roermond areas were inaccessible, while rail and road links used to transport fuels were disrupted by submerged tracks and bridges. Vitol Holding BV temporarily suspended operations at its Maas terminals, citing safety concerns for staff and equipment.

“We took immediate action to safeguard our people and assets,” a Vitol Holding BV representative said. “Although the disruption was significant, our teams acted quickly to restore operations as soon as conditions allowed.”

Industry analysts estimate that up to 15 percent of the Netherlands’ daily refined product throughput was affected at the peak of the flooding. “The logistical bottlenecks created localized shortages and delayed shipments, particularly for inland clients,” said Pieter van Haastert, an energy sector consultant.

Unions representing oil and gas workers reported no serious injuries, but highlighted the strain on staff called in to manage emergency procedures. “Our members worked long hours under difficult conditions to ensure safe shutdowns and restarts,” said Marieke Jansen of the Dutch Energy Workers Union.

By late August 2021, most affected facilities had resumed normal operations, with repairs and upgrades to flood defenses underway. No disruptions are currently reported.
